summary: Generalizes the technique of using a packet's TTL or hop limit to check that it came from a directly connected neighbor. Packets that arrive with a lower value than expected are rejected. It obsoletes the experimental RFC 3682 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: GTSM helps protect directly connected routing sessions by checking how many router hops a packet has crossed. Peers send with TTL 255, and the receiving router can treat packets arriving with a lower value as suspicious.

questions: why does gtsm drop packets with low ttl
subtitle: A TTL check that helps protect directly connected routing peers from remote packets.

tldr.problem: Forged control packets can consume router resources. Protocol peers are often adjacent, so packets from farther away should have a lower TTL or Hop Limit after passing through routers.
tldr.mechanism: GTSM-enabled peers send packets with TTL or Hop Limit 255. The receiver classifies packets for a configured session by whether the received value is expected and can separate or discard dangerous packets.
tldr.outcome: GTSM provides a simple defense for single-hop sessions but does not replace authentication. RFC 5082 obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3682.

today: RFC 5082 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes Experimental RFC 3682. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 5082.

sections.title: What GTSM Protects
sections.content:
The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) helps protect a router's IP control plane from attacks that consume CPU or other scarce resources. It uses the IP TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit to check whether a packet could have come from an adjacent peer.

GTSM is not a substitute for authentication and does not protect against insider attacks such as spoofing or replay by an on-path attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: GTSM checks whether a packet could have traveled from a directly connected peer without passing through another router. It can reduce some remote attacks, but it does not replace authentication.

sections.title: Assumptions Behind the Check
sections.content:
GTSM assumes that most protocol peerings are between adjacent routers, both peers support the mechanism, and the router can separate packets into resource pools. Classification needs to happen before packets consume the scarce resource that GTSM is meant to protect.

Routers along the path must decrement TTL correctly. Tunnels must not allow an attacker to hide a packet's distance, and unfiltered interfaces are treated as trusted because directly connected attackers can still interfere.
sections.plainLanguage: The check works only when routers handle TTL normally and packets are classified before they use scarce resources. It also depends on secure tunnel handling and protection from attackers on the local link.

sections.title: Sending and Classifying Packets
sections.content:
For an enabled session, every related IP packet MUST be sent with TTL 255, including related ICMP error messages. If GTSM is added to an existing protocol, it SHOULD NOT be enabled by default for backward compatibility.

On receipt, the router classifies packets as Unknown, Trusted, or Dangerous. By default, it SHOULD keep Dangerous packets from competing for resources with other categories, MUST NOT drop Trusted or Unknown packets through GTSM processing, and MAY drop Dangerous packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets for an enabled session are sent with TTL 255. The receiver separates packets with an expected TTL from packets tied to the session that arrive with an unexpected TTL.

sections.title: Limits of TTL-Based Protection
sections.content:
Each router on a normal IP path decrements TTL by one, so a remote sender cannot normally deliver a packet with TTL 255 to a directly connected peer. A tunnel can weaken this property if it preserves an inner TTL and terminates at the protected peer.

Non-initial IP fragments may not contain enough transport information to identify their session. The RFC strongly recommends that GTSM-protected protocols avoid fragmentation, for example by adjusting the MTU or using Path MTU Discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: The TTL check is useful for direct peers, but tunnels and fragmented packets can make the source harder to classify. The RFC recommends avoiding fragmentation for GTSM-protected protocols.

sections.title: Where GTSM Applies
sections.content:
The RFC limits its defined procedure to single-hop sessions, especially directly connected peers. A multi-hop deployment might accept a configured range of TTL values, but the RFC does not specify that behavior and says it needs further experimentation.

RFC 5082 obsoletes RFC 3682 and clarifies that related ICMP messages are also sent and checked with TTL 255. Those related messages are not reliably delivered, but can be used to disturb a session.
sections.plainLanguage: GTSM is defined most clearly for directly connected peers. The RFC does not standardize a multi-hop version and tightens the rule for related ICMP messages.
